content: Drugs that act on the renin-angiotensin system, such as trandolapril, can cause harm to a developing fetus, including injury and death. This is particularly concerning when used during the second and third trimesters of pregnancy. These drugs can impair fetal renal function, leading to oligohydramnios, which may result in complications such as fetal lung hypoplasia and skeletal deformities. Neonatal complications may include skull hypoplasia, anuria, hypotension, renal failure, and even death. If pregnancy is detected, trandolapril should be discontinued immediately. In rare cases where no alternative treatment is available, the mother should be informed of the risks, and serial ultrasounds should be performed to monitor the fetus. If oligohydramnios is observed, the drug should be stopped unless it is deemed lifesaving for the mother. Infants exposed to trandolapril in utero should be closely monitored for hypotension, oliguria, and hyperkalemia. Trandolapril is associated with a range of adverse effects, some of which are serious. For example, angioedema has been reported, particularly in Black patients, at a higher rate than in non-Black patients. Angioedema can involve the face, extremities, lips, tongue, glottis, or larynx. Laryngeal edema can be life-threatening and requires immediate discontinuation of the drug, emergency treatment with subcutaneous epinephrine, and close monitoring. Intestinal angioedema has also been reported, presenting as abdominal pain with or without nausea or vomiting. This condition resolves after discontinuation of the drug and should be considered in the differential diagnosis of patients on ACE inhibitors presenting with abdominal pain. Hypotension is another potential adverse effect of trandolapril, particularly in patients who are volumeor salt-depleted due to diuretics, dietary restrictions, dialysis, diarrhea, or vomiting. Symptomatic hypotension is rare in uncomplicated hypertensive patients but may occur in those with congestive heart failure or renal insufficiency. In such cases, therapy should be initiated under close medical supervision, and patients should be monitored during the first two weeks of treatment or after any dosage adjustments. If hypotension occurs, the patient should be placed in a supine position, and intravenous saline may be administered if necessary. A transient hypotensive response does not preclude further treatment, but dose adjustments may be required. Trandolapril, like other ACE inhibitors, has been associated with neutropenia and agranulocytosis, particularly in patients with renal impairment or collagen-vascular diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus or scleroderma. Periodic monitoring of white blood cell counts is recommended in these patients. Rarely, ACE inhibitors have been linked to cholestatic jaundice, which can progress to fulminant hepatic necrosis and death. Patients who develop jaundice while on trandolapril should discontinue the drug and seek immediate medical attention. Hyperkalemia has been reported in approximately 0.4% of hypertensive patients treated with trandolapril. Risk factors include renal insufficiency, diabetes mellitus, and the use of potassium-sparing diuretics, potassium supplements, or potassium-containing salt substitutes. These should be used cautiously, if at all, with trandolapril. Persistent nonproductive cough is another known side effect of ACE inhibitors, likely due to the inhibition of bradykinin degradation. This cough resolves upon discontinuation of the drug. Patients undergoing major surgery or anesthesia with agents that induce hypotension may experience additional risks with trandolapril, as it blocks the formation of angiotensin II. Hypotension in these cases can be corrected with volume expansion. Adverse reactions such as headache and fatigue have been reported in more than 1% of patients but are generally mild and manageable. In patients with impaired renal function, trandolapril may cause changes in renal function, particularly in those with severe heart failure or renal artery stenosis. Increases in blood urea nitrogen and serum creatinine have been observed but are usually reversible upon discontinuation of the drug. Renal function should be monitored during the initial weeks of therapy, especially in patients with preexisting renal impairment or those on diuretics. Elevations in liver enzymes and bilirubin have been reported in a small percentage of patients. Persistent elevations may necessitate discontinuation of the drug. Rarely, eosinophilic pneumonitis has been associated with ACE inhibitors. Post-marketing data have identified additional adverse reactions, including myocardial infarction, angina, arrhythmias, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, pancreatitis, hepatitis, agranulocytosis, and renal failure. Laboratory findings have shown occasional increases in creatinine, blood urea nitrogen, and liver transaminases, as well as rare cases of thrombocytopenia and hyponatremia. In summary, trandolapril is an effective medication for managing hypertension and heart failure but carries significant risks, particularly in certain populations.
